hero.description: Autonomous agents need more than payments. They need credit, programmable acceptance rules, and verifiable settlement — all without a central counterparty. Ergo is one of the few settlement layers with the protocol-level primitives needed for this.

problem.heading: Merchant checkout rails solve commerce.
problem.headingMuted: Autonomous work settlement needs another layer.

stripeProblemItems.title: No persistent identity
stripeProblemItems.body: Commerce rails are built around persistent buyers, merchants, accounts, disputes and compliance. Autonomous work flows can be temporary processes acting under bounded authority.

stripeProblemItems.title: One-time payments only
stripeProblemItems.body: Autonomous services often need bounded credit: issue now, redeem later, expire by policy. That is a settlement primitive, not only a checkout event.

stripeProblemItems.title: No programmable acceptance
stripeProblemItems.body: A work rail needs terms inside the claim: accept only if the task hash, verifier receipt, deadline and policy match. Otherwise payment and verification split apart.

stripeProblemItems.title: Millisecond economics break
stripeProblemItems.body: Small machine calls need deterministic costs and receipt retention. Human checkout systems can coexist with this, but they do not replace the programmable settlement layer.

creditUnlock.heading: Verifiable workflows are table stakes. Programmable credit is the unlock.
creditUnlock.description: A verifiable workflow proves that work happened. Programmable credit lets agents coordinate future work before final settlement: sub-agent budgets, task-conditioned Notes, reserve-backed claims, expiry rules and policy-constrained spending.
creditUnlock.formula: Payments move value. Verification proves work. Credit creates economic agency.

items.title: Payments
items.body: Agents pay for API calls, compute, data and tools without forcing every decision back through a human checkout.

items.title: Verification
items.body: Receipts, task hashes and acceptance predicates define whether the agreed work actually happened.

items.title: Credit
items.body: Bounded, redeemable Notes let agents coordinate work now and settle later under explicit rules.

whyErgoItems.title: eUTXO: verifiable atomicity
whyErgoItems.body: Transactions are deterministic against explicit inputs and outputs. Agents can reason about outcomes before submitting, with no protocol-level reentrancy and less exposure to common account-model MEV patterns.

whyErgoItems.title: ErgoScript: programmable trust
whyErgoItems.body: Acceptance predicates are first-class primitives. 'Accept this note only if task hash matches and deadline hasn't passed' — one script, on-chain, trustless.

whyErgoItems.title: Babel Fees: agents don't need ERG
whyErgoItems.body: Agents can cover transaction fees through supported token-to-ERG paths. That reduces the need to pre-fund every new agent instance with ERG — critical for ephemeral compute.

whyErgoItems.title: Sigma Protocols: private credit
whyErgoItems.body: Zero-knowledge proofs are native. Agents can prove they hold a credential or completed a task without revealing which agent they are.

whyErgoItems.title: Proof-of-Work: no chain halts
whyErgoItems.body: PoW has no governance emergency stops. Agent infrastructure built on Ergo won't be frozen by a validator cartel or foundation decision.

whyErgoItems.title: Native tokens: community money
whyErgoItems.body: Issue native tokens and design Note/Reserve-style payment patterns without ERC-20-style deployment ceremony. Specific agent-payment contracts remain prototype/testnet-first unless audited.

stack.heading: The agent economy stack
stack.description: Ergo mainnet provides the base settlement layer and Babel-fee-style fee abstraction. Accord, ChainCash/Basis and Note/Reserve/Tracker reference implementations are testnet-first prototypes unless a specific deployment is audited and explicitly marked production-ready.

stackLayerItems.label: Reserves
stackLayerItems.description: On-chain capital backing — holds ERG or tokens as collateral for issued notes

stackLayerItems.label: Trackers
stackLayerItems.description: Verifiable accounting — track balances, credit limits, redemption history

stackLayerItems.label: Notes
stackLayerItems.description: Programmable IOUs — issue, transfer, and redeem off-chain money

stackLayerItems.label: Trust Rules
stackLayerItems.description: Acceptance logic — 'accept this note only under these rules' — fully on-chain

stackLayerItems.label: Reputation
stackLayerItems.description: Agent reputation without a central oracle — active research area

stackLayerItems.label: Identity
stackLayerItems.description: Persistent agent identity across sessions without deanonymisation

useCases.heading: Three composable flows. Two testnet reference flows, one upcoming.

useCaseItems.title: LLM buys inference
useCaseItems.flow: Agent → issues note → API provider accepts predicate → delivers tokens
useCaseItems.detail: One call, one proof, no persistent account. Provider sets their own acceptance rules — minimum task hash, maximum credit, deadline.

useCaseItems.title: Agent pays on credit
useCaseItems.flow: Reserve deployed → notes issued against it → tracker monitors usage → auto-settle
useCaseItems.detail: Credit limit enforced on-chain. No counterparty risk — the reserve contract is the bank.

useCaseItems.title: Community currency
useCaseItems.flow: Reserve holds ERG → community issues local notes → acceptance predicates define rules
useCaseItems.detail: A local marketplace, a compute cooperative, or an agent network — each with their own money and trust rules.

bml.heading: We're building the reference stack.
bml.description: Notes, credit, trackers, reserves, acceptance predicates — and the showcase for agent-to-agent settlement receipts. If you're building in this space, we want to talk to you.
